skills.name: Measure the specific heat capacity of a liquid and calculate with Q = mcΔθ

note.text:
Electrical method for a liquid: a known mass of liquid in a lagged calorimeter is heated by an immersion heater.
Electrical energy supplied = VIt (or power × time). If heat losses are ignored, VIt = (m_liquid c_liquid + m_cal c_cal)Δθ.
Ignoring the calorimeter, c = VIt / (mΔθ).
Reduce errors by lagging the calorimeter, stirring, and starting a few degrees below room temperature so that the gain and loss of heat roughly cancel.
In any mixture problem: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold bodies.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to find the specific heat capacity of a liquid by the electrical method and calculate heat, time or temperature change with Q = mcΔθ.
Builds on: Lesson {3} (Q = mcΔθ and c for a solid) and Form Three electrical energy.
Leads to: Lesson {5}, where heat changes the state of a substance without changing its temperature.

sections.heading: The electrical method
sections.text:
• Weigh the empty calorimeter, then weigh it again with the liquid: the difference is the mass of liquid.
• Put in an immersion heater, a stirrer and a thermometer, and lag the calorimeter.
• Take the starting temperature, switch on, and record the voltage V and current I.
• After a measured time t, stir and take the highest temperature.
Electrical energy supplied = VIt. If losses are ignored, VIt = mcΔθ, so c = VIt ÷ (mΔθ).
A more careful answer includes the calorimeter: VIt = (m_liq c_liq + m_cal c_cal)Δθ.

sections.heading: Errors and calculations
sections.text:
Heat escaping to the room is the main error. It makes Δθ smaller than it should be, so the calculated c comes out too large. Lagging, stirring, a lid and a short heating time all reduce it. Starting a few degrees below room temperature lets the heat gained at the start cancel the heat lost at the end.
Typical calculations with Q = mcΔθ:
• Heat needed: {1} kg of water by {50} K is {1} × {4200} × {50} = {210000} J.
• Time on a {2000} W heater: {210000} ÷ {2000} = {105} s.
• Rise given the heat: Δθ = Q ÷ (mc).

key_words.meaning: an electric heater placed in the liquid
insulation around a calorimeter to reduce heat loss
electrical energy: voltage × current × time, in joules

examples: a {1000} W heater for {84} s gives {84000} J
{84000} J into {1} kg of water raises it {20} K

mistake.wrong: heat lost to the room makes the measured c too small
mistake.right: it makes the measured c too large
mistake.why: The energy supplied is still counted in full, but the temperature rise is smaller, and c = VIt ÷ (mΔθ).

worked_example.problem: A {P} W heater warms {m} kg of a liquid for {t} s and the temperature rises by {dt} K. Find the specific heat capacity of the liquid.
steps: Energy supplied = power × time = {P} × {t} = {P * t} J.

cards.idea: Electrical energy supplied = VIt, or power × time.
example: a {500} W heater for {60} s supplies {30000} J

cards.idea: Ignoring losses: VIt = mcΔθ, so c = VIt ÷ (mΔθ).
example: {30000} J into {0.5} kg raising it {20} K: c = {3000} J/(kg·K)

check.prompt: A {P} W heater warms {m} kg of a liquid for {t} s; the temperature rises by {dt} K. Find c for the liquid, in J/(kg·K).

misconceptions.explain: Divide by the mass as well.
Divide by the temperature change as well.

cards.idea: Lagging, stirring and a short heating time reduce heat lost to the room.
example: without lagging, the measured c comes out too large

pick.q: The calorimeter is not lagged, so heat escapes to the room. How does this affect the value found for c?
pick.r: It comes out too large, because some of the energy counted did not reach the liquid
w: It comes out too small, because the liquid gets less energy
It is not affected, because the energy supplied is measured exactly
It comes out too large, because the temperature rise is bigger
e: The energy VIt is counted in full, so the calculated c is too large, not too small.
The energy is measured exactly, but not all of it reaches the liquid.
Losing heat makes the temperature rise smaller, not bigger.
pick.y: All of VIt is counted but Δθ comes out small, and c = VIt ÷ (mΔθ).

pick.q: Why is the liquid stirred during the electrical method?
pick.r: So that the whole liquid is at one temperature when the thermometer is read
w: To make the liquid heat up faster
To stop the liquid from boiling
To spread the electrical current through the liquid
e: Stirring moves heat about but does not add energy, so it does not speed up the heating.
The liquid is not heated to its boiling point in this experiment.
The current stays in the heater; it does not pass through the liquid.
pick.y: Without stirring, the liquid near the heater is hotter than the rest and the reading is too high.

pick.q: Why is the experiment often started a few degrees below room temperature?
pick.r: Heat gained from the room at the start then roughly cancels the heat lost to it at the end
w: Cold liquid has a larger specific heat capacity
The heater works better in a cold liquid
It makes the temperature rise larger
e: Specific heat capacity hardly changes over such a small range of temperature.
The heater supplies the same power whatever the temperature of the liquid.
The rise measured is the same; what changes is how the losses cancel.
pick.y: Below room temperature heat flows in; above it heat flows out. Starting below makes the two roughly cancel.

pick.q: Why should the heating time be kept fairly short?
pick.r: The longer the liquid stays hot, the more heat escapes to the room
w: A long time would use too much electricity
A long time would melt the calorimeter
The heater can only run for a short time
e: The cost of the electricity is not a source of error in the measurement.
The temperatures reached are far below the melting point of the calorimeter.
An immersion heater can run for much longer than the experiment needs.
pick.y: Heat loss grows with the time spent above room temperature, so a short run keeps the error small.

questions.prompt: A heater of power {P} W runs for {t} s. How much energy does it supply, in joules?

misconceptions.explain: The time is already in seconds: do not divide by {60}.

questions.prompt: An immersion heater takes {I} A from a {V} V supply for {t} s. Find the electrical energy supplied, in joules.

misconceptions.explain: Multiply by the time {t} s as well.
Multiply by the current {I} A as well.

questions.prompt: A {P} W heater warms {m} kg of a liquid for {t} s; the temperature rises by {dt} K. Find c for the liquid, in J/(kg·K).

misconceptions.explain: Divide by the mass as well.
Divide by the temperature change as well.

questions.prompt: How long must a {P} W heater run to raise {m} kg of water (c = {4200} J/(kg·K)) by {dt} K, if no heat is lost?

misconceptions.explain: Divide the energy by the power to get the time.
Include the specific heat capacity {4200} J/(kg·K).

solution: Heat needed Q = mcΔθ = {m} × {4200} × {dt} = {heatMC(m, 4200, dt)} J.
